what: Plexus builds electronic products for other companies. It designs, engineers and manufactures complete devices — surgical instruments, aircraft systems, industrial controls, laboratory equipment — for customers who own the brand and sell the product. It specialises in complex, low-volume, highly regulated products rather than consumer electronics.
customers: Medical device companies, aerospace and defence manufacturers, and industrial equipment makers who need products built to exacting standards in modest quantities.
money: Surgical devices, diagnostic equipment and laboratory instruments.
Factory automation, semiconductor equipment and industrial controls.
Avionics, defence electronics and related systems.
moat: Building a medical device or an avionics system requires regulatory qualification of the manufacturing process itself, which takes a long time and cannot be moved casually to another supplier. Once Plexus is qualified to build a surgical instrument, the customer would need to requalify everything to switch — so programmes stay for their product’s life, often a decade or more.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $28.9M, which for a contract manufacturer reflects inventory and receivables building as revenue grows.
A net margin of 4.1% is the structural reality of contract manufacturing: the customer owns the brand and takes the margin.
The shares trade at about 28.2 times earnings and 16.1 times EV/EBITDA, which is a high price for this kind of business.
Revenue is concentrated in programmes, and a customer losing its own market or insourcing production removes revenue abruptly.
Only five analysts cover the stock, so the $307.80 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Revenue grew sharply to $5.0B in 2026 from $4.0B, after three flat years.
Regulatory qualification of the manufacturing process makes programmes extremely sticky once won.
Cash of $281.2M against $240.2M of debt is a clean balance sheet for a manufacturer.
The complex, low-volume, regulated niche is far less exposed to price competition than consumer electronics manufacturing.
Healthcare is the largest segment and its demand is structurally growing and largely non-cyclical.
watch: Revenue by segment and operating margin. Contract manufacturing lives on a thin margin, so the margin on growing revenue tells you whether the growth is worth having.
view: Contract electronics manufacturing is structurally a thin-margin business — the customer owns the brand, the intellectual property and the customer relationship, and takes the corresponding share of the economics. Plexus earns a 4.1% net margin, which is approximately what this industry earns, and no amount of execution changes that fundamental split. What execution can change is which contracts you get, and that is where Plexus has made a sensible choice.

Rather than competing for high-volume consumer work where price is everything, Plexus specialises in complex, low-volume, heavily regulated products: surgical instruments, avionics, laboratory equipment. The crucial feature of these is that the manufacturing process itself requires regulatory qualification. Once Plexus is approved to build a particular surgical device, switching supplier means requalifying the entire process with regulators — an expense and a delay no medical device company accepts to save a few per cent. Programmes therefore stay for the product’s life, often a decade.

The segment mix is good. Healthcare is the largest piece and its demand is structurally growing and largely indifferent to the economy. Aerospace and defence is long-cycle and well funded. Industrial is the cyclical part, including semiconductor equipment, which swings hard. Revenue jumped to $5.0 billion in 2026 after three flat years, and the negative free cash flow is the familiar signature of a manufacturer building inventory and receivables to serve growth rather than a sign of trouble.

Where I part company with the market is price. At 28.2 times earnings and 16.1 times EV/EBITDA for a business that structurally earns 4% net margins, you are paying a quality multiple for an industry that does not usually get one. The stickiness is real and justifies a premium to Jabil or Flex; it does not justify this much. Five analysts with a $308 average on a $209 price is thin scrutiny behind an optimistic view. I would want to see the operating margin expanding on that higher revenue before paying it.
bull: Regulatory qualification locks in decade-long programmes in healthcare and aerospace, revenue growth continues, and operating margin expands on scale.
bear: A structural 4% margin meets a 28 times earnings multiple, semiconductor and industrial demand turns down, and a major programme insources or loses its own market.
